focused_checks.evidence: Initial E_P, equation (1.27), equation (1.28), and the maximum-speed relation retain every coefficient, square, equality, radical and physical symbol. Only upright descriptive subscripts change from \mathrm{м} to \mathrm{m}; equation-label numbers remain 1.27 and 1.28.

The model explicitly assumes a horizontal Hookean spring, negligible spring mass and resistance, fixed support and no external drive. Displacement is measured from equilibrium and elastic potential energy is zero there. Within this undriven horizontal spring model, equilibrium is the undeformed spring position, so E_P=kx^2/2 is consistent. Constant height makes gravitational potential energy a removable constant; it is not incorrectly claimed to vary or vanish physically.

Mechanical energy belongs to the ball-plus-spring system, not the ball alone. Negligible spring mass leaves the ball's translational kinetic energy and spring elastic potential energy. Resistance, external drive and support work are excluded; internal dissipation is explicitly excluded rather than assuming every closed system conserves mechanical energy.

Release from rest at the right-hand amplitude is followed by increasing speed and decreasing elastic potential energy toward equilibrium, maximum speed there, then decreasing speed and increasing elastic potential energy toward the left-hand turning point. At that point speed and kinetic energy are zero. Both left-moving stages use 速率, not an incorrect increase/decrease of signed v_x; the squared horizontal velocity component is separately explained.

At either turning point kinetic energy is zero and total energy equals maximum elastic potential energy; at equilibrium elastic potential energy is zero and total energy equals maximum kinetic energy. These maxima occur at different positions, not simultaneously. Substituting v_m=sqrt(k/m)x_m gives (m/2)(k/m)x_m^2=kx_m^2/2, confirming equation (1.28).

The proportionalities E proportional to x_m^2 and E proportional to v_m^2 are explicitly limited to the same ideal system with fixed m and k. The text warns against discarding m or k when comparing different systems. The continuation p0037#1 completes this source claim without importing n12 material.

The retained pendulum analogy identifies gravitational potential energy as the energy exchanged with kinetic energy. It does not apply the spring's kx^2/2 formula to the pendulum or claim unrestricted large-angle simple harmonic motion.
